d: The AlignPosition constraint applies force to move two attachments together, or to move one attachment to a goal position.
h:
For an overview on creating, visualizing, and simulating mover constraints, including AlignPosition, see mover constraints. Also see Roblox units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

An AlignPosition constraint applies force to move two attachments together, or to move one attachment to a goal position. As indicated by the name, it only affects the position of the attachments, not their orientation (to align attachments by orientation, see AlignOrientation).

By default, the constraint only applies force to Attachment0, although this behavior can be controlled through the constraint's reactionary force.

Force location

By default, force is applied to the parent of Attachment0 at that attachment's location, meaning that if the parent's center of mass is not aligned with the direction of the force, torque will be applied as well as force. Alternatively, force can be applied to the parents' center of mass by toggling on ApplyAtCenterOfMass.

Force magnitude

You can configure the AlignPosition constraint to apply the maximum force that constraints allow through the RigidityEnabled property. When true, the physics solver reacts as quickly as possible to complete the alignment. When false, the force is determined by MaxForce, MaxVelocity, and Responsiveness.

Reactionary force

By default, the constraint only applies force to Attachment0 while Attachment1 remains unaffected. If desired, force can be applied to both attachments in equal and opposite directions by enabling ReactionForceEnabled.

Attachment mode

The Mode property specifies whether the constraint uses one or two attachments in calculating its goal. By default, this is TwoAttachment, meaning that the constraint disregards Position and attempts to move Attachment0 to the position of Attachment1. If set to OneAttachment, the constraint disregards Attachment1 and attempts to move Attachment0 to Position.

kid.simple: This page explains `AlignPosition`, a constraint that pulls a part toward a target spot. It can pull one attachment to another attachment, or pull one attachment to a position you type in. It only moves the part, it does not turn it. It is useful for floating pets, hover boards, and objects that follow a player.
kid.analogy: It is like a magnet on a string pulling a toy car toward your hand: it moves the car to you, but it does not care which way the car is facing.
keyPoints: `AlignPosition` applies force to move `Attachment0` to a goal position. It changes position only, never rotation.
To line up rotation instead, use `AlignOrientation`.
By default only `Attachment0` gets pushed. Turn on `ReactionForceEnabled` to push both attachments toward each other with equal and opposite force.
Force is applied at the attachment's spot. If that spot is off-center, the part can also start to tip or spin. Turn on `ApplyAtCenterOfMass` to push from the center instead.
`RigidityEnabled = true` makes it snap to the goal as fast as physics allows.
With `RigidityEnabled = false`, you control how strong and fast it is with `MaxForce`, `MaxVelocity`, and `Responsiveness`.
`Mode = OneAttachment` ignores `Attachment1` and moves `Attachment0` to the `Position` you set.

terms.constraint: An object that controls how parts move, like an invisible motor, rope, or hand pushing them. Mover constraints push or spin parts for you.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are welded or joined together so physics moves them as one piece. A car body plus its welded seats is one assembly.
terms.attachment: A small invisible point you put inside a part. Constraints hook onto attachments, the same way a rope ties onto a hook.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachment slots a constraint uses. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed; Attachment1 is the other end or the reference point.
terms.goal position: The spot the constraint is trying to reach, like (0, 20, 0), which is 20 studs above the world center.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Push there and it slides without spinning; push off to the side and it also turns.
terms.rigidity: How stiff or instant the pull is. Rigid means it tries to reach the goal right away.
terms.responsiveness: How quickly the constraint reacts. A higher number means it chases the goal faster.
terms.equal and opposite: Both parts get the same amount of push but in opposite directions, so they pull toward each other, like two people tugging the same rope.
terms.MaxVelocity: The top speed the constraint is allowed to move the part, in studs per second.

example.title: Make a block float to a spot in the sky
example.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace (part not Anchored)
example.code:
local part = script.Parent

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local align = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
align.Attachment0 = attachment
align.Mode = Enum.PositionAlignmentMode.OneAttachment
align.Position = Vector3.new(0, 20, 0) -- 20 studs above the world center
align.MaxForce = 100000
align.MaxVelocity = 10 -- move at most 10 studs per second
align.Responsiveness = 20
align.Parent = part
explain: We add an attachment for the constraint to pull on.
`Mode = OneAttachment` means we only use one attachment and aim it at `Position`.
`Position = (0, 20, 0)` is the goal spot in the world.
`MaxForce`, `MaxVelocity`, and `Responsiveness` decide how strong and how quick the pull is, because `RigidityEnabled` is off.
Once parented, the block rises and settles at the goal.

watchOut: In `TwoAttachment` mode, changing `Position` does nothing. Switch `Mode` to `OneAttachment` first.
If the part tips over while moving, the force is being applied off-center. Turn on `ApplyAtCenterOfMass` or add an `AlignOrientation`.
If `MaxForce` is too low, a heavy part may never lift off. Raise it or turn on `RigidityEnabled`.
